summary:
Objective

To evaluate the effectiveness of a physical activity coaching intervention compared with text messaging intervention and waitlist control in adults with mobility limitations.

Design

Three arm, pragmatic, superiority, hybrid type 1 effectiveness implementation randomised controlled trial.

Setting

Health services and general communities across five Australian states, 19 December 2018 to 7 March 2023.

Participants

512 community dwelling adults (≥18 years) who self-reported mobility limitations (difficulty or inability to walk 800 m, with or without a walking aid) but were still able to leave home without physical assistance from another person.

Interventions

Participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1:1 allocation ratio to: a six month, multicomponent intervention including fortnightly physiotherapist delivered telephone coaching (coaching group, n=172); a six month, multicomponent intervention including regular unidirectional text messages (texting group, n=171); and no intervention for six months, followed by the six month text messaging intervention (waitlist control group, n=169). Participants and physiotherapists were unmasked to group allocation.

Main outcome measure

The primary outcome was device measured mean daily steps at six months, analysed according to treatment allocation using all available data. Outcome assessors and data analysts were masked to group allocation.

Results

Participants' mean age was 69 years (standard deviation (SD) 10 years) and 76% (n=388/511) were women. More than half (n=263/508, 51%) of participants reported multiple long term conditions as the main reason for their mobility limitation. At six months, mean daily steps were 931 higher (95% confidence interval 409 to 1452 steps; P=0.001) in the coaching group (mean 7256 (SD 3736) steps) compared with waitlist group (6526 (3003) steps); and 571 steps higher (58 to 1084, P=0.03) compared with the texting group (6529 (3029) steps). Mean daily steps in the texting group were 359 higher (-91 to 810, P=0.12) compared with the waitlist group, but this was not statistically significant. The number of adverse events was similar between groups (11/172 (6%) in the coaching group, 7/171 (4%) in the texting group, and 13/169 (8%) in the waitlist group) and none were serious.

Conclusion

A person centred coaching intervention produced modest increases in physical activity and was more effective than a less intensive texting intervention or no intervention among adults with mobility limitations.

Trial registration

Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry ACTRN12618001983291.
title: Physical activity coaching and text messaging for adults with mobility limitations (ComeBACK): hybrid type 1 effectiveness implementation randomised controlled trial.

summary:
Objective

To determine whether intrapartum hyoscine butylbromide, sodium bicarbonate, and their combination increase the rate of spontaneous vaginal birth in nulliparous women undergoing induction of labour.

Design

Multicentre, randomised, double blind, placebo controlled, 2×2 factorial phase 3 trial (SAINT).

Setting

11 Norwegian hospitals providing comprehensive obstetric care.

Participants

Nulliparous women aged 18-50 years with a singleton live fetus in cephalic presentation at term with an indication for induction of labour.

Interventions

Participants were randomly assigned (1:1:1:1) to oral sodium bicarbonate (4×1 g per dose) plus intravenous hyoscine butylbromide (20 mg per dose), oral sodium bicarbonate plus intravenous placebo, oral placebo plus intravenous hyoscine butylbromide, or double placebo. The investigational medicinal product was administered at the onset of active labour and repeated every four hours to a maximum of three doses.

Main outcome measure

Spontaneous vaginal birth (no instrumental or caesarean delivery).

Results

Between 4 January 2023 and 29 January 2025, 3094 nulliparous women were randomised, and 2963 comprised the full analysis set. Spontaneous vaginal birth occurred in 57% (422/741) in the bicarbonate plus hyoscine butylbromide arm, 61% (445/734) in the bicarbonate arm, 61% (449/741) in the hyoscine butylbromide arm, and 56% (422/747) in the double placebo arm. Marginal risk differences for spontaneous vaginal birth compared with double placebo were -0.2 (95% confidence interval -5.1 to 4.7; P=0.93) percentage points for combined treatment, 3.1 (-1.7 to 8.0; P=0.21) percentage points for bicarbonate, and 4.0 (-0.8 to 8.9; P=0.10) percentage points for hyoscine butylbromide. Serious adverse events were similar between groups, and no treatment related serious morbidity or deaths were observed.

Conclusions

No clear evidence was found that intrapartum hyoscine butylbromide, sodium bicarbonate, or their combination increased spontaneous vaginal birth compared with placebo. Although small beneficial effects cannot be excluded, the findings do not support routine intrapartum use of either agent to facilitate spontaneous vaginal birth after induction of labour.

Trial registration

European Clinical Trials Database (EudraCT; 2021-000392-37); EU Clinical Trials Information System (CTIS; EU CT number 2024-511848-55-00); ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05719467).
title: Effect of intrapartum hyoscine butylbromide and sodium bicarbonate on spontaneous vaginal birth in nulliparous women after induction of labour (SAINT): multicentre randomised placebo controlled factorial trial.

summary: Plastic pollution is a critical environmental and public health challenge, with growing evidence linking human exposure to microplastics, nanoplastics, and associated chemicals to adverse health outcomes. This review summarises current knowledge on the health effects of plastic exposure, addressing both established findings and critical knowledge gaps. We examine human exposure to plastics and associated health risks based on available clinical and epidemiological evidence. Additionally, we explore chemicals associated with plastic, including their potential as carcinogens and disruptors of endocrine and immune function. Recognising the urgent need for preventive measures, we examine emerging strategies for reducing plastic burdens, including global regulatory efforts like the United Nations Plastics Treaty and proposed public health guidelines. By integrating current evidence, this review aims to provide a foundation for advancing research and informing strategies to mitigate health risks associated with plastic.
title: Effects of plastic exposure on human health.

summary:
Objective

To evaluate the effect of intensive compared with standard treatment of systolic blood pressure (SBP) on cognitive outcomes and brain structures in adults with type 2 diabetes.

Design

Multicentre, open label, outcome assessor masked, randomised controlled trial.

Setting

145 clinical centres across seven geographical regions in China.

Participants

12 821 adults aged ≥50 years with type 2 diabetes, raised SBP, and increased cardiovascular risk, of whom 12 434 without probable dementia at baseline were included in this cognitive ancillary study. Further assessments were performed annually and at the end of study.

Interventions

Participants were randomly assigned to receive intensive treatment targeting SBP <120 mm Hg or standard treatment targeting SBP <140 mm Hg for up to five years.

Main outcome measures

The primary cognitive outcome was a composite of all cause dementia or mild cognitive impairment. Secondary cognitive outcomes included all cause dementia, mild cognitive impairment, changes in cognitive functions, and changes in brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) characteristics. A subset of participants underwent brain MRI at baseline (n=862) and at the end of study (n=605) to assess changes in white matter lesion volume and total brain volume.

Results

6219 participants were assigned to receive intensive treatment and 6215 to receive standard treatment. Baseline mean age was 63.7 years, and 5567 (44.8%) participants were women. After one year, mean SBP was 121.6 mm Hg in the intensive treatment group and 133.2 mm Hg in the standard treatment group. During a median follow-up of 3.8 years, the primary cognitive outcome of all cause dementia or mild cognitive impairment occurred in 747 participants (3.69 events per 100 person years) in the intensive treatment group and 783 participants (3.89 events per 100 person years) in the standard treatment group (hazard ratio 0.96, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.86 to 1.06; P=0.38). In the MRI substudy (428 intensive treatment v 434 standard treatment), the intensive treatment group had a smaller increase in white matter lesion volume compared with the standard treatment group (between group difference -0.09 inverse hyperbolic sine (asinh) transformed cm3, 95% CI -0.15 to -0.02; P=0.01).

Conclusions

Over a median of about four years, no statistically significant difference in incidence of a composite of all cause dementia or mild cognitive impairment was observed among adults with type 2 diabetes receiving standard treatment of SBP (target <140 mm Hg) and intensive treatment (target <120 mm Hg). Intensive treatment was, however, associated with a reduction in the accrual of cerebral white matter lesion volume.

Trial registration

ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03808311.
title: Effect of intensive blood pressure control on cognitive outcomes and brain structures in adults with type 2 diabetes: prespecified analysis of secondary outcomes of BPROAD randomised controlled trial.

summary:
Objective

To determine whether discontinuing versus continuing angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) on the morning of surgery reduces perioperative hypotension in older patients undergoing non-cardiac surgery.

Design

Multicentre, randomised, double blind, placebo controlled trial.

Setting

Five tertiary teaching hospitals in China, November 2020 to December 2023.

Participants

2036 older patients (60-80 years) using ACE inhibitors or ARBs for at least two weeks and scheduled for non-cardiac surgery under general anaesthesia.

Interventions

Patients were randomised to receive their usual ACE inhibitor or ARB or a placebo in identical capsules on the morning of surgery.

Main outcome measures

The primary outcome was the incidence of perioperative hypotension (mean blood pressure <65 mm Hg or a ≥30% decrease from baseline requiring treatment). Secondary outcomes included duration of hypotension, requirement for a vasopressor, intraoperative fluid volume, postoperative hypotension, and 30 day complications (neurocognitive disorders, major cardiocerebral events) or mortality.

Results

2012 patients (mean age 68.8 years; 54.4% male) completed the study: 1004 were included in the antihypertensive group and 1008 in the no antihypertensive group. The incidence of perioperative hypotension was lower in the no antihypertensive group (314/1008, 31.2%) versus antihypertensive group (457/1004, 45.5%): adjusted odds ratio 0.52 (95% confidence interval (CI) 0.43 to 0.63); absolute risk difference -14.4% (95% CI -18.5% to -10.1%); P<0.001. The duration of hypotension and requirement for a vasopressor were both reduced in the no antihypertensive group: adjusted mean difference -1.3 minutes (95% CI -1.8 to -0.8 minutes) and 28.5% v 41.1%; adjusted odds ratio 0.54 (95% CI 0.44 to 0.66). Intraoperative fluid volume, postoperative hypotension, 30 day complications, and mortality did not differ significantly between groups.

Conclusions

Discontinuing ACE inhibitors or ARBs on the morning of surgery in older patients with hypertension statistically significantly reduced perioperative hypotension and the requirement for vasopressors without increasing 30 day complications or mortality. This simple strategy provides high certainty evidence for preoperative drug management in this patient population.

Trial registration

Chinese Clinical Trial Registry ChiCTR2000039376.
title: Effect of discontinuing antihypertensives on perioperative hypotension in older patients before non-cardiac surgery: multicentre, randomised, double blind, controlled trial.

summary:
Objectives

To evaluate trends in pregabalin use and overdose in Australia and examine temporal relationships with media coverage (December 2018), prescribing and dispensing restrictions (April 2020), and boxed warnings (February 2021).

Design

Retrospective observational study of dispensing and overdose data, with changepoint, interrupted time series, and latent class analysis.

Setting and participants

Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme data (PBS; 10% random sample of people with drug subsidies) and overdose calls (self-harm, recreational use, and misuse) reported to Australia's largest Poisons Centre (50% national sample), 2016-24.

Main outcome measures

Population adjusted rates of dispensing and overdose, timing of breakpoints and rate ratios, proportion of people who use pregabalin at high risk of misuse.

Results

227 864 people were dispensed 3 441 851 pregabalin prescriptions in the PBS 10% sample and 4871 pregabalin overdose calls were made to the Poisons Centre. Pregabalin use peaked in 2018 before plateauing and declining. Three breakpoints were found in dispensing data, with major decreases in level and slope: December 2018, May 2020, December 2021. The combined rate ratio for dispensing was 0.748 (95% confidence interval 0.700 to 0.800). Compared with the projected historical trend in the absence of interventions (counterfactual), approximately 118 390 (93 960 to 140 940) fewer pregabalin prescriptions were recorded nationally in December 2021, and an ongoing reduction of 0.7% (0.5% to 0.9%) was found each month. All breakpoints were associated with declines in overdose rates, with a combined rate ratio of 0.532 (95% CI 0.406 to 0.695). This reduction corresponded to approximately 41.3 (26.9 to 52.4) fewer pregabalin overdose calls in December 2021 and an ongoing reduction of 1.6% (1.0% to 2.3%) each month. Latent class analysis of 57 744 people dispensed pregabalin in the 12 months after the final breakpoint revealed four groups. The high risk group (7790, 13.5%) were more likely male, younger, dispensed more pregabalin, with shorter refill interval and high rates of opioids and benzodiazepine co-use (5120 (65.7%) and 2455 (31.5%), respectively).

Conclusions

Pregabalin use and overdose in Australia have declined in recent years. Major decreases in trend corresponded with media coverage (December 2018) and prescribing and dispensing restrictions (May 2020). The third breakpoint may be a delayed impact of boxed warnings (implemented February 2021). These findings suggest that regulatory and risk communication measures may contribute to reducing pregabalin related harm.
title: Changes in pregabalin use and overdose after government interventions and media coverage: retrospective observational study.

summary:
Objectives

To evaluate the effectiveness of paravertebral blockade versus thoracic epidural during the perioperative period in reducing chronic post-thoracotomy pain.

Design

Open label, parallel group, superiority, multicentre, randomised controlled trial.

Setting

15 thoracic centres in the UK.

Participants

Adult patients undergoing thoracotomy randomised (1:1) to either paravertebral blockade or thoracic epidural using a web based service between January 2019 and September 2023.

Interventions

Participants in the paravertebral group received three single-shot paravertebral injections of local anaesthetic before incision followed by placement of a paravertebral catheter. Participants in the epidural group had a thoracic epidural catheter placed and loaded with local anaesthetic before incision.

Main outcome measure

The primary outcome was incidence of chronic post-thoracotomy pain at six months after randomisation, defined as a 100 mm visual analogue score greater than or equal to 40 mm (indicating moderate pain) when considering worst chest pain over the past week. Secondary outcomes included acute pain (visual analogue score of 100 mm) and complications.

Results

770 patients were enrolled, of which 428 (56%) were male (mean (standard deviation, SD) age 66.6 (11.0) years). After 33 exclusions of patients after randomisation who did not proceed to thoracotomy, 737 remained in the modified intention-to-treat population (364 in the paravertebral group, 373 in the epidural group). Six months after randomisation, 59 (22%) of 272 participants in the paravertebral group and 47 (16%) of 292 participants in the epidural group developed chronic post-thoracotomy pain (adjusted risk ratio 1.32 (95% confidence interval (CI) 0.93 to 1.86), adjusted risk difference 0.05 (95% CI -0.01 to 0.11), P=0.12). During the acute phase, worst and average pain was greater on day 1 with paravertebral blockade (adjusted mean difference 7.7 mm (95% CI 2.8 to 12.5 mm) and 7.0 mm (95% CI 2.7 to 11.2 mm), respectively), but no different on days 2-3. Hypotension was less common in the paravertebral group than the epidural group (12% v 18%, respectively, adjusted risk ratio 0.66 (95% CI 0.46 to 0.94), adjusted risk difference -0.06 (95% CI -0.11 to -0.01)), as was pruritis (4% v 12%, adjusted risk ratio 0.37 (95% CI 0.21 to 0.64), adjusted risk difference -0.07 (95% CI -0.11 to -0.03)), although more participants in this group experienced urinary retention (12% v 6%, adjusted risk ratio 2.21 (95% CI 1.35 to 3.61), adjusted risk difference 0.05 (95% CI 0.01 to 0.09)), complications were similar otherwise.

Conclusions

Paravertebral blockade did not reduce chronic post-thoracotomy pain at six month follow-up compared to thoracic epidural. Thoracic epidural provided marginally better acute pain relief one day after the operation, but showed no difference thereafter. Postoperative complications were comparable between groups. The findings support the ongoing use of both techniques.

Trial registration

ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03677856.
title: Thoracic epidural versus paravertebral blockade for reducing chronic post-thoracotomy pain (TOPIC-2): open label, parallel group, superiority, multicentre, randomised controlled trial.

summary:
Objective

To assess the effect of ventilation with a laryngeal mask airway (LMA) compared with endotracheal tube (ETT) on perioperative respiratory adverse events (PRAEs) in children undergoing adenotonsillectomy.

Design

Multicentre, randomised, parallel group trial.

Setting

Four tertiary hospitals in China, 2023-24.

Participants

400 children aged ≥2 years and <7 years who were scheduled for adenotonsillectomy under general anaesthesia.

Interventions

Participants were randomised 1:1 to receive ventilation with a laryngeal mask airway (n=200) or an endotracheal tube (n=200) during adenotonsillectomy.

Main outcome measure

The primary outcome was the proportion of participants who developed any perioperative respiratory adverse event (PRAE): laryngospasm, bronchospasm, desaturation, airway obstruction, severe cough, or stridor in the intention-to-treat population.

Results

400 children (mean age 4.7 (standard deviation 1.0) years; 155 (38.7%) girls) were enrolled between 24 May 2023 and 4 April 2024, with last follow-up on 4 May 2024. LMA was converted to ETT in three participants. Overall, 22.5% (45/200) participants in the LMA group experienced PRAEs versus 57.5% (115/200) in the ETT group (absolute risk difference -35.0 percentage points, 95% confidence interval -43.5 to -25.7; P<0.001). The LMA group had fewer PRAEs in both the intraoperative (9.0% (18/200) v 17.5% (35/200); -8.5, -15.2 to -1.8; P=0.01) and the postoperative period (16.5% (33/200) v 49.5% (99/200); -33.0, -41.2 to -24.0; P<0.001). The LMA group also had a lower proportion of participants with laryngospasm (0.0% v 3.0%; P=0.03), desaturation (15.0% v 28.0%; P=0.002), airway obstruction (3.5% v 12.5%; P<0.001), and severe cough (10.5% v 42.0%; P<0.001). Neither group experienced serious adverse events.

Conclusion

Ventilation with an LMA by experienced anaesthesiologists resulted in fewer perioperative respiratory adverse events than ventilation with an ETT in children undergoing adenotonsillectomy.

Trial registration

Chictr.org.cn ChiCTR2300071399.
title: Perioperative respiratory adverse events in children undergoing adenotonsillectomy with laryngeal mask airway versus endotracheal tube ventilation: multicentre, randomised controlled trial.

summary:
Objective

To compare the benefits and harms of therapeutic interventions for adhesive capsulitis.

Design

Systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.

Data sources

Medline, Cochrane Library, Embase, Web of Science, and Scopus were searched from inception to 1 May 2025, with an update in November 2025.

Eligibility criteria for selecting studies

Randomised controlled trials enrolling adults with adhesive capsulitis, comparing active treatment with another intervention, placebo, or usual care.

Main outcome measures

Pain, function, range of motion, and adverse events.

Results

A total of 189 randomised controlled trials involving 12 988 participants and 59 interventions were included. Most trials contributing to principal outcomes were at high risk of bias (71% for pain, 72% for function, and 71% for range of motion). At short term follow-up, moderate certainty evidence suggested that extracorporeal shockwave therapy probably reduced pain compared with usual care (mean difference -1.97 on a 0-10 scale, 95% confidence interval (CI) -2.97 to -0.97). Low certainty evidence suggested that extracorporeal shockwave therapy may improve function (mean difference -11.42 on a 0-100 scale, 95% CI -16.68 to -6.15), although direct and indirect estimates were limited by important incoherence. For short term range of motion, moderate certainty evidence suggested that manipulation under anaesthesia combined with intra-articular steroid injections probably improved flexion (mean difference 33.29°, 95% CI 11.19° to 55.39°), as did manipulation under anaesthesia alone (26.16°, 8.19° to 44.13°). Low certainty evidence suggested that extracorporeal shockwave therapy may improve flexion (22.42°, 12.99° to 31.84°) and abduction (18.62°, 8.09° to 29.14°), but both comparisons were limited by important incoherence. At mid-term follow-up, evidence for possible improvements in function with extracorporeal shockwave therapy and flexion with passive mobilisation was of low certainty, while evidence for pain reduction with extracorporeal shockwave therapy was of very low certainty. Most other comparative estimates were supported by low or very low certainty evidence. Comparative safety remained highly uncertain because adverse events were incompletely and inconsistently reported; the absence of reported adverse events should not be interpreted as evidence of absence of harm.

Conclusion

Moderate certainty evidence suggests short term pain reduction with extracorporeal shockwave therapy and improved short term flexion with manipulation under anaesthesia, with or without intra-articular steroid injections. Most other treatment effects remain uncertain because of low certainty and incoherence, and comparative safety and mid-term effects are poorly established. The available evidence is mainly short term and outcome specific. Longer term comparative effectiveness, overall benefits and harms, and applicability beyond predominantly primary adhesive capsulitis remain uncertain.

Systematic review registration

PROSPERO CRD420251070468.
title: Interventions for adhesive capsulitis: systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.

summary:
Objective

To describe the epidemiological characteristics, public health response, and evidence of international spread of a large measles outbreak that contributed to the loss of Canada's measles elimination status.

Design

Descriptive analysis of the cohort of measles outbreak cases reported to Ontario's public health surveillance system during the outbreak period: epidemiological week of 28 October 2024 to 6 October 2025.

Setting

Ontario, Canada.

Participants

Individuals meeting the outbreak case definition for confirmed or probable measles infection during the outbreak period.

Exposure

Exposure to measles virus associated with the Ontario outbreak and related transmission chains.

Main outcome measures

Demographic characteristics, vaccination status, admission to hospital, complications, pregnancy associated outcomes, mortality, and evidence of international spread based on measles virus genotyping and sequencing. Cases were identified using an outbreak-specific case definition incorporating epidemiological, clinical, laboratory, and viral sequencing criteria. Phylogenetic analysis of measles virus sequences was used to assess evidence of onwards spread to other countries.

Results

The outbreak consisted of 2377 cases (2064 confirmed and 313 probable) over 49 weeks and contributed to the loss of Canada's measles elimination status. Most cases (2146/2377, 90.3%) occurred among members of historically under-vaccinated communities, with limited spillover into the broader population. Among the 2377 cases, approximately three quarters of cases (n=1736, 73.0%) occurred in individuals aged 19 years or younger, 2121 (89.2%) were unvaccinated, and 97 (4.1%) had unknown vaccination status. The outbreak was associated with 166 (7%) admissions to hospital, 13 (<1%) admissions to intensive care unit, 51 (2.1%) infections during pregnancy, 10 (<1%) congenital measles infections, one (<1%) case of encephalitis, and one (<1%) infant death. Sequencing identified a novel N450 distinct sequence identifier that was subsequently detected in countries including the United States of America, Mexico, and the Netherlands. The outbreak strain was designated a World Health Organization named strain (MVs/Ontario.CAN/47.24).

Conclusions

These findings highlight the risk of measles re-establishment in countries that have attained elimination and underscore the importance of culturally appropriate community engagement to build trust in immunisation and prevent future outbreaks. This outbreak shows the fragility of measles elimination in the presence of long standing immunity gaps within interconnected communities across the Americas and the population-level protection that limited broader community transmission.
title: Impact of a large measles outbreak associated with transmission in the Americas and Canada's loss of measles elimination status: descriptive cohort study.

summary:
Objective

To test the efficacy and cost effectiveness of high volume injections with and without corticosteroid versus sham injection for midportion Achilles tendinopathy.

Design

Single centred, participant and assessor masked, three arm randomised controlled trial (Inject trial).

Setting

Community.

Participants

From 5 December 2019 and 24 July 2022, 192 adults (18 years or older) diagnosed with midportion Achilles tendinopathy were randomly assigned (1:1:1) to sham (n=64), high volume injection without corticosteroid (n=63), or high volume injection with corticosteroid (n=65).

Interventions

Participants were allocated to sham injection (2-3 mL 0.5% bupivacaine hydrochloride), high volume injection with corticosteroid (50 mL saline and 0.5% bupivacaine with 25 mg hydrocortisone in the first 10 mL), or high volume injection with no corticosteroid (same solution but without hydrocortisone). They received the same exercise programme, education, and activity modification advice.

Main outcome measures

The primary clinical outcome was pain and disability using the validated VISA-A and the primary endpoint was at 52 weeks. The economic outcome was cost per quality-adjusted life-years from a societal perspective.

Results

VISA-A data were obtained from 181 (94%) of 192 participants at 12 months. No clear differences were noted between sham and high volume injection either with (-3.5 (98.33% confidence interval -12.0 to 5.0)) or without corticosteroid (4.0 (-4.2 to 12.3)), and between the two injections (-7.5 (-15.3 to 0.3)), at 12 months. The point estimate was closest to the target difference for the comparison between injections and favoured the arm without steroid. The only differences observed on VISA-A at intermediate time points were a benefit for high volume with corticosteroid versus sham at six weeks (9.2 (1.5 to 16.9)) but worse outcomes for high volume injection with corticosteroid versus high volume injection with no corticosteroid at 26 weeks (-8.6 (-16.4 to -0.7)). The health economic analysis found high volume injection with corticosteroid to be less costly than the sham with similar effectiveness based on quality-adjusted life-years (>0.90 probability of being cost effective at $AUD50 000 and $100 000 willingness-to-pay thresholds). No serious trial related adverse events were recorded.

Conclusion

High volume injections with or without corticosteroids did not improve pain or disability compared with sham at 12 months. Although high volume injections with corticosteroid showed short term clinical benefit and potential reduction in healthcare costs over a year, they were associated with worse longer term clinical outcomes. The clinical data do not support routine use for high volume injections with corticosteroid for midportion Achilles tendinopathy.

Trial registration

Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry ACTRN12619001455156.
title: Efficacy and cost effectiveness of high volume injections with and without corticosteroid compared with sham for midportion Achilles tendinopathy (Inject trial): randomised controlled trial.

summary:
Objective

To compare the clinical effectiveness of three splints after repair of zone 1 and 2 flexor tendons: forearm based (long), Manchester short (short), and relative motion flexion (mini) splints.

Design

Prospective, randomised, parallel group, pragmatic, superiority, clinical trial.

Setting

26 UK hospitals.

Participants

430 participants (aged ≥16 years) requiring rehabilitation after primary repair of zone 1 and 2 flexor tendons in one or two fingers of the hand according to British Society for Surgery of the Hand guidelines.

Interventions

Participants were randomly assigned 1:1:1 to the long, short, or mini splint. Splints were worn continuously for five weeks and intermittently for a further week at night and in vulnerable situations such as public environments. Masking participants was not possible owing to the nature of the intervention.

Main outcome measures

The primary outcome was the mean post-randomisation score on the patient-rated wrist and hand evaluation (PRWHE) instrument at 6, 12, 26, and 52 weeks, analysed by intention to treat.

Results

430 participants were randomised to the long splint (n=143), short splint (n=140), or mini splint (n=147) and 403 were included in the intention-to-treat analysis. Adherence, defined as wearing the splint for a minimum of five weeks, was 83% (118/143) for the long splint, 76% (106/140) for the short splint, and 78% (115/147) for the mini splint. Mean post-randomisation PRWHE scores were 24.5 (standard deviation 15.5) in the long splint group, 23.5 (16.7) in the short splint group, and 22.4 (15.0) in the mini splint group, with adjusted between group differences of 0.3 (98.3% confidence interval -4.0 to 4.6, P=0.88) for the long versus short splint, 2.3 (-1.9 to 6.5, P=0.19) for the long versus mini splint, and 2.0 (-2.2 to 6.3, P=0.25) for the short versus mini splint. Serious adverse event rates occurred in 10% (14/143) of participants in the long splint group, 11% (15/140) in the short splint group, and 11% (16/147) in the mini splint group.

Conclusion

This trial found no statistically significant difference in clinical effectiveness between the long, short, and mini splint. Apart from some small differences, secondary outcomes were comparable across all three groups.

Trial registration

ISRCTN Registry ISRCTN10236011.
title: Comparative effectiveness of three splints for rehabilitation after finger flexor tendon repair (FIRST): randomised controlled trial.

summary: Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is the most common form of kidney cancer, with 435 000 patients newly diagnosed worldwide each year. In addition to morphology and histology, molecular subtyping has advanced the diagnostic classification of RCC. Contemporary diagnosis relies on cross sectional imaging in the form of computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging and selective biopsy. For localised disease, nephrectomy remains the standard of care, with partial nephrectomy being an option for smaller tumours. Ablation or stereotactic radiation is appropriate for selected patients. Adjuvant pembrolizumab provides improved disease-free and overall survival in high risk clear cell RCC. In metastatic disease, the introduction of immune checkpoint inhibitor based combinations has extended overall survival, providing a durable response in some patients. Despite these advances, primary and secondary resistance, along with the lack of predictive and prognostic biomarkers, remain a challenge.
title: Advances in the management of renal cell carcinoma.

summary:
Objective

To assess the added value of acetic acid chromoendoscopy (AAC) for the detection of dysplasia and oesophageal adenocarcinoma during Barrett's oesophagus surveillance endoscopies.

Design

Prospective, open label, stepped wedge cluster, randomised trial.

Setting

18 Dutch community hospitals.

Participants

Patients undergoing surveillance for Barrett's oesophagus were eligible, excluding those with known or previously treated dysplasia.

Interventions

Hospitals randomly shifted from surveillance without AAC (control) to AAC (intervention), with endoscopists trained before implementation. Targeted biopsies were obtained if lesions were present; random four quadrant biopsies were conducted.

Main outcome measures

The primary endpoint was the neoplasia detection rate, defined as the percentage of participants with low grade dysplasia, high grade dysplasia, and oesophageal adenocarcinoma in any biopsy, confirmed by an experienced gastrointestinal pathologist. The secondary endpoint was the neoplasia detection rate in targeted biopsies.

Results

2267 participants were included, of whom 1438 (63%) were allocated to surveillance without AAC and 829 (37%) to surveillance with AAC; AAC was applied in 679 (82%) allocated participants. Overall, neoplasia was diagnosed in 163 (7.2%) participants (111 (4.9%) low grade dysplasia, 30 (1.3%) high grade dysplasia, and 22 (1.0%) oesophageal adenocarcinoma). AAC use did not increase the neoplasia detection rate (7.4% (50/679) with AAC versus 7.1% (113/1588) without AAC; odds ratio 0.97, 95% confidence interval 0.65 to 1.44; adjusted for calendar time and Barrett's oesophagus length). Suspected lesions were detected in 95 (14.0%) participants receiving AAC versus 101 (6.4%) without AAC (P<0.001), but the targeted neoplasia detection rate was not higher (2.1% (14/679) versus 1.8% (29/1588); odds ratio 1.05, 0.49 to 2.24).

Conclusions

Use of AAC did not improve detection of neoplasia in patients with Barrett's oesophagus undergoing endoscopic surveillance in routine clinical practice.

Trial registration

www.onderzoekmetmensen.nl; NL-OMON25059 (prospective registration; 4 Dec 2019).
title: Acetic acid chromoendoscopy for detection of neoplastic Barrett's oesophagus: stepped wedge cluster randomised controlled trial (ACID-trial).

summary:
Objective

To evaluate whether providing authors with a manuscript template structured according to the Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials (SPIRIT) 2025 reporting guideline for use during revision improves the completeness of reporting in randomised trial protocols.

Design

Randomised controlled trial.

Setting

BMJ Open.

Population

70 of 74 manuscripts screened between 29 April and 27 May 2025 that reported randomised controlled trial protocols with a decision of minor or major revision after the first round of peer review were randomly allocated (1:1) using an R generated sequence. Authors were not informed of the study.

Interventions

Handling editors asked the intervention group authors to use a SPIRIT based manuscript template when preparing their first revision. The template included structured subheadings corresponding to SPIRIT 2025 items, along with guidance on reporting. Editorial decisions were not conditional on use of the template. Control group manuscripts underwent standard peer review.

Main outcome measures

The primary outcome was completeness of reporting score in the revised manuscript (adjusted for baseline), calculated as the mean of 11 SPIRIT items that are frequently inadequately reported (each scored 0, 0.5, or 1) and linearly rescaled to a 0-10 score. After submission of their first revision, authors in the intervention group completed an online survey. The survey included both fixed response and open ended questions designed to capture the authors' perceptions of ease of use, helpfulness, and any challenges encountered when using the template. Secondary outcomes included mean completeness of reporting scores for each item, median time to submission of the revised manuscript, and authors' experiences of using the template. Outcome assessors, but not editors or investigators, were masked.

Results

Of the 70 manuscripts randomised (35 in each group), all were analysed, with no loss to follow-up. In the intervention group, completeness of reporting in randomised trial protocols improved by 0.61 points (95% confidence interval 0.20 to 1.01) compared with the control group, with mean (standard deviation) scores increasing from 5.42 (1.07) to 6.70 (1.23) and 5.77 (1.19) to 6.32 (0.94), respectively. The largest improvements were observed for recruitment, data collection methods, and access to data. Median time to submission of the first revision was similar between the intervention and control groups (27.10 v 29.86 days, respectively). Data on harms were not systematically collected. Among 14 of 35 survey respondents (40%), many (8/13, 62%) reported the template as time consuming and some (5/13, 39%) as burdensome. Most respondents, however, found it easy to use (10/13, 77%), helpful for improving the manuscript (9/13, 69%), and reassuring for adherence to SPIRIT (13/13, 100%).

Conclusions

Providing authors of randomised controlled trials with a SPIRIT based template during manuscript revision modestly improved the completeness of reporting in the trial protocols without extending revision times.

Trial registration

Open Science Framework 10.17605/OSF.IO/C4YQZ.
title: Effectiveness of a structured template to improve completeness of reporting randomised trial protocols: randomised controlled trial.

summary:
Objectives

To evaluate the accuracy and completeness of adverse event summary reports for medical devices and compliance of the reports with the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) requirements.

Design

Cross sectional study.

Setting

The FDA manufacturer and user facility device experience (MAUDE) database.

Participants

All adverse event summary reports filed in MAUDE from July 2019 to June 2025.

Main outcome measures

Identification of device problem codes, appropriate identification as summary reports in the submission form, concordance between the number of events data field and the report narrative, and compliance with FDA reporting deadlines.

Results

6308 summary reports were submitted to MAUDE containing 159 503 adverse events. Use of summary reports increased from 808 to 1757 between 2020 and 2024, a factor of 1.21 per year (P<0.001). Most (91%) adverse events in summary reports were for class 3 high risk devices. Summary reports lacked descriptions of potential device related problems: 57% of reports denoted an "adverse event without identified device or use problem" and 38% of reports selected "insufficient information" in the device problem code data field. Manufacturers incorrectly checked "N" (no) in the summary report (Y/N, reporting yes/no) field for 694 summary reports (11%) and erroneously listed "n=1" under the number of events field for 423 summary reports (7%), causing an undercount of 11 902 adverse events. The majority (55%) of summary reports failed to comply with the FDA reporting deadline of 30 days after the manufacturer became aware of the adverse event.

Conclusions

Adverse event summary reports in MAUDE are frequently incomplete, inaccurate, and delayed. Improvements are needed to ensure timely identification of device safety signals and uphold FDA transparency standards.
title: Evaluation of the accuracy, completeness, and compliance of current summary reporting of adverse events to the Food and Drug Administration using the manufacturer and user facility device experience (MAUDE) database: cross sectional study.

summary: Climate change and biodiversity loss are global environmental crises driving emerging infectious diseases, including bat-borne pathogens of public health significance: Ebola, Marburg, Nipah, Hendra, classic rabies virus, and Australian bat lyssavirus, as well as the fungus Histoplasma This review presents the evidence on the mechanisms of transmission, impact, and prevention and management strategies relevant to each of these pathogens. Transmission pathways vary between pathogens but often involve exposure to body fluids or excreta of a bat or other infected animal or human. The diseases associated with these infections have high mortality rates, and survivors may continue to experience a range of long term effects, including neurological and neuropsychiatric signs and symptoms. Prevention strategies may be implemented to reduce the risk of zoonotic spillover and human-to-human transmission of these pathogens, including better ecological stewardship, reducing exposure of domestic animals and humans to bats, isolation of infected people, and, where possible, vaccination of humans and animals. The mainstay of treatment for these conditions is supportive care; however, specific drugs are now available for histoplasmosis and Ebolavirus infection. In the face of climate change and further loss of biodiversity, developing more effective strategies to prevent and manage these conditions will be critical.
title: Bat-borne zoonoses: transmission, impact, prevention, and management.

summary:
Objective

To characterise the reporting completeness of clinical trials involving large language model (LLM) interventions using established reporting guidelines.

Design

Systematic review and meta-research analysis.

Data sources

Bibliographic databases (Embase, Medline, and CENTRAL) were searched for trial reports and protocols, and trial registries (ClinicalTrials.gov and World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform) were searched for trial registrations published from 1 January 2017 to 6 December 2025.

Eligibility criteria

Trial reports, trial protocols, and trial registrations describing clinical trials of LLM interventions in medicine. LLM interventions used for a healthcare function in a clinical trial setting included patient education, clinical documentation, communication support, triage, care navigation, management recommendations, or clinical decision support. Eligible studies prospectively assigned human participants to the intervention and evaluated a health related biomedical or behavioural outcome.

Main outcome measures

Overall study level and item level reporting completeness assessed using reporting guidelines matched to study design and purpose, including TRIPOD-LLM (Transparent Reporting of a multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis Or Diagnosis-LLM), CONSORT (Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials) 2025 and CONSORT-AI, SPIRIT (Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials) 2025 and SPIRIT-AI, CHART (Chatbot Assessment Reporting Tool), and the WHO Trial Registration Dataset (version 1.3.1). Two reviewers independently screened and extracted trial and intervention characteristics, and three calibrated raters assessed item level reporting completeness.

Results

The systematic search yielded 461 records, including 68 trial reports, 15 protocols, and 378 registrations. Trial reports were predominantly small sample, single site randomised studies published between 2024 and 2025, spanning diverse clinical specialties and primarily targeting patient facing education and management recommendations. Mean reporting completeness was modest across eligible trial reports (TRIPOD-LLM 40%, CONSORT 2025 44%, CONSORT-AI 59%, CHART 52%), trial protocols (SPIRIT 2025 51%, SPIRIT-AI 57%), and trial registrations (WHO Trial Registration Dataset 61%). Clinical trial reports of LLM interventions prioritise narrative framing and commentary over the methodological detail needed for replication, risk-of-bias assessment, and governance of model performance over time. Critical methodological elements for reproducibility, including data and intervention provenance, input preprocessing, model versioning and access modality, inference parameters, output postprocessing, as well as protocol, data, and code access, were inconsistently reported. Harms planning, monitoring, and reporting were often incompletely reported, limiting the critical appraisal of the safety of LLM interventions in healthcare.

Conclusion

Clinical trials of LLM interventions show modest adherence to established reporting guidelines, with persistent underreporting of LLM specific methodological details, reproducibility artefacts (protocols, data, code), and harms reporting required to support reproducibility and confident appraisal of safety risks before their clinical translation.
title: Reporting completeness of clinical trials evaluating large language model interventions in medicine: systematic review.

summary:
Objective

To evaluate the association between quadrivalent human papillomavirus vaccination before pregnancy and subsequent risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes.

Design

Nationwide, population based matched case-control study.

Setting

Population of Sweden, from 1 January 2006 to 31 December 2023.

Participants

624 713 singleton births among nulliparous women aged 16-35 years in Sweden between 2006 and 2023; 92 620 (14.8%) women had received quadrivalent human papillomavirus vaccination before pregnancy.

Main outcome measures

Risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes associated with quadrivalent human papillomavirus vaccination, with preterm birth (<37 weeks), including its subtypes, and spontaneous preterm birth as primary outcomes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes, prelabour rupture of membranes, small for gestational age infant (<10th centile), severe small for gestational age infant (<3rd centile), stillbirth, and neonatal mortality as secondary outcomes. Effect modification by age at human papillomavirus vaccination was assessed. Conditional logistic regression was used to estimate odds ratios and adjusted odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).

Results

After adjustment for confounders, quadrivalent human papillomavirus vaccination was associated with lower odds of all included adverse pregnancy outcomes. Statistically significant associations were observed for preterm birth (<37 weeks) (adjusted odds ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.91 to 0.99), very preterm birth (28 weeks to 31 weeks) (0.85, 0.75 to 0.97), spontaneous preterm birth (0.95, 0.91 to 0.99), preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (0.93, 0.87 to 1.00), and severe small for gestational age infant (0.92, 0.87 to 0.97). Risk reduction was generally more pronounced among women vaccinated at younger ages.

Conclusions

Quadrivalent human papillomavirus vaccination before pregnancy was associated with a lower risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes, particularly among women vaccinated at earlier ages, extending benefits of human papillomavirus vaccination beyond cancer prevention.
title: Quadrivalent human papillomavirus vaccination before pregnancy and pregnancy outcomes: nationwide, population based case-control study.

summary:
Objective

To evaluate the early comparative effectiveness of robotic versus conventional total knee replacement (TKR) and unicompartmental knee replacement (UKR) in the UK.

Design

Target trial emulation study.

Setting

Public and private hospitals using data from the National Joint Registry of England, Wales, Northern Ireland, the Isle of Man, Guernsey, and Jersey.

Participants

697 145 knee replacement surgeries between 2018 and 2024: 675 034 were conventional (TKRs and UKRs) and 22 111 were robotic.

Main outcome measures

The main outcome was five year knee replacement survival (mean 2.5 years follow-up); all cause revision risk; cause specific revision risk; intraoperative complications; and revision complexity of robotic versus conventional (TKR and UKR) knee replacement. Kaplan-Meier and Cox regression analyses were used to compare implant survival and indications for revision surgery. Propensity score matching using target trial emulation framework was used to estimate the average treatment effect in the treated population.

Results

The five year implant survival of the matched conventional and robotic TKR groups was 98.5% (95% confidence interval (CI) 98.3% to 98.7%) and 98.6% (98.2% to 99.0%), respectively, with no between group difference in revision risk (hazard ratio 1.03, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.26; P=0.71). The five year implant survival of the matched conventional and robotic UKR groups was 97.8% (95% CI 97.2% to 98.3%) and 96.4% (92.4% to 98.3%), respectively, with no between group difference in revision risk (hazard ratio 1.03, 95% CI 0.75 to 1.42; P=0.86). Cause specific revision risk and intraoperative complication risks did not differ between groups for either TKR or UKR.

Conclusions

No statistically significant differences were detected in revision risk, cause specific risk, or intraoperative complication risk between the robotic and conventional groups. This was consistent for both TKR and UKR. The possibility of unmeasured and residual confounding cannot be ruled out, however, owing to the observational design of the study. These results highlight the importance of careful evaluation of robotic technology in publicly funded healthcare systems, given the substantially higher capital and procedural costs involved.
title: Early national comparison of robotic versus conventional knee replacements for arthritis using National Joint Registry data: target trial emulation study.

summary:
Objectives

To evaluate the early comparative effectiveness of robotic versus conventional total hip replacement (THR) in the UK.

Design

Target trial emulation study.

Setting

Public and private hospitals using data from the National Joint Registry of England, Wales, Northern Ireland, the Isle of Man, Guernsey, and Jersey.

Participants

666 283 THRs performed between 2018 and 2024; 656 080 were conventional THRs and 10 203 were robotic THRs.

Main outcome measures

Five year THR implant survival (mean 2.5 year follow-up), all cause revision risk, cause specific revision risk, malpositioning revision risk, intraoperative complications, and patient survival up to five years. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis, Cox proportional hazards regression, and Fine and Gray models were used. Propensity score matching created comparable treatment groups to estimate the average treatment effect in the treated population.

Results

The five year implant survival of the matched conventional and robotic THR groups was 98.8% (95% confidence interval (CI) 98.6% to 99.0%) and 98.8% (CI 98.3% to 99.1%), respectively, with no difference in revision risk between groups (hazard ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.75 to 1.22; P=0.73). Cause specific revision risk and intraoperative complication risks did not differ between groups. However, a significantly lower risk of revisions related to implant malposition (dislocation, leg length discrepancy, and malalignment) was observed in the robotic group (hazard ratio 0.53, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.93; P=0.03). The five year patient survival of the matched conventional and robotic THR groups was 96.3% (95% CI 95.8% to 96.8%) and 96.2% (95.2% to 97.0%), respectively, with no difference in all cause mortality risk (hazard ratio 1.12, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.34; P=0.17).

Conclusions

No significant differences were found in overall THR or patient survival, cause specific revision, or intraoperative complication risks between robotic and conventional groups. Robotic THR was associated with a lower revision risk from causes related to implant malpositioning. However, the possibility of unmeasured and residual confounding cannot be ruled out owing to the observational design. These results highlight the importance of careful evaluation of robotic technology in publicly funded healthcare systems because of the substantially higher capital and procedural costs.
title: Early national comparison of robotic versus conventional hip replacements for arthritis using National Joint Registry data: target trial emulation study.

summary: In 1788, the Birmingham physician William Withering was consulted by an apothecary in Wellington, Shropshire, about the case of a woman, Mrs Houlston, whom Erasmus Darwin's son, Robert Darwin, a medical practitioner in Shrewsbury, had attended the day before. Withering thought that Darwin's prescription had been inappropriate and changed it. Robert reacted angrily, and a vituperative correspondence followed. Erasmus, Robert's father, also medically qualified, may have been involved in the affair, by urging his son to attack Withering and by helping him to write his letters. Erasmus may have had good reason for wanting to damage Withering's reputation. Although all three of them were alumni of the Edinburgh Medical School in the latter half of the 18th century, albeit at different times, and although Erasmus had recommended Withering to both a post in Birmingham and membership of the Lunar Society, he may have become jealous of Withering's success as a physician and botanist. The enmity between them had culminated in a dispute over the treatment of a patient in Staffordshire, whom Withering was asked to see after Erasmus had attended her, with little therapeutic success. Withering recommended digitalis, which seemed to have saved her life. Darwin reported the case in 1780, anonymously including it in a posthumous publication credited to another medical son, Charles, and without crediting Withering. In turn, Withering responded by criticising Darwin in his 1785 monograph An Account of the Foxglove The rift between the two seems to have been irreparable.
title: When I use a word . . . Alumni of the Edinburgh Medical School 1726-2026: Erasmus Darwin versus William Withering.

summary:
Objectives

To investigate associations between current use of menopausal hormone therapy and development of venous thromboembolism, ischaemic stroke, and myocardial infarction.

Design

Nationwide nested case-control study.

Setting

National Danish health registries.

Participants

9807 women with venous thromboembolism, 18 460 women with ischaemic stroke, and 11 974 women with myocardial infarction were identified in a cohort of women of 50-69 years living in Denmark between 2003 and 2021 without a medical history of venous thrombosis, arterial thrombosis, cancer, liver disease, thrombophilia, oophorectomy, infertility treatment, endometriosis, or polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS, previously known as polycystic ovary syndrome). Cases were matched by birth year to a total of 49 035, 92 300, and 59 870 women without thrombotic disease, respectively.

Main outcome measures

Receiving a first time diagnosis of venous thromboembolism, ischaemic stroke, or myocardial infarction.

Results

Among women who had not used menopausal hormone therapy, incidence rates of venous thromboembolism, ischaemic stroke, and myocardial infarction per 10 000 person years were 15.8, 20.3, and 13.0, respectively. Compared with no current use, current use of oral oestrogen therapy (alone or combined with progestin) was associated with increased rates of venous thromboembolism (hazard ratio 1.6, 95% CI 1.5 to 1.8), ischaemic stroke (1.3, 1.2 to 1.4), and myocardial infarction (1.2, 1.1 to 1.3). The absolute risk increase per year was 0.09% (95% confidence interval (CI) 0.08 to 0.13%) for venous thromboembolism, 0.06% (0.04 to 0.08%) for ischaemic stroke, and 0.03% (0.01 to 0.04%) for myocardial infarction, corresponding to numbers needed to harm for one year of use of 1055 (95% CI 791 to 1266), 1642 (1232 to 2463), and 3846 (2564 to 7692), respectively.Use of oral forms of oestradiol was consistently associated with increased venous thromboembolic risk compared with no current use. Oral oestradiol doses >1 mg/day used for more than one year was associated with increased risks of ischaemic stroke and myocardial infarction, with risks increasing with treatment duration (stroke hazard ratio 1.8, 95% CI 1.4 to 2.2 and myocardial infarction hazard ratio 1.8, 1.4 to 2.4 for >5 years of use compared with no current use).Transdermal therapy was not associated with increased thrombotic rates compared with no current use, with the exception of increased risk of myocardial infarction with transdermal combined cyclic therapy (hazard ratio 2.1, 95% CI 1.1 to 4.1).

Conclusions

Compared with no current use of any hormone therapy, oral menopausal hormone therapy was associated with increased venous thromboembolic risk regardless of dosage and treatment duration, while prolonged use of high dose oral oestradiol (>1 mg/day) showed elevated risks of ischaemic stroke and myocardial infarction. No increased thrombotic risks were observed with transdermal therapy.
title: Contemporary menopausal hormone therapy and thrombotic disease: nationwide nested case-control study.

summary:
Objective

To compare the effect of specific antidepressants with placebo on heart rate corrected QT interval (QTc) during the first eight weeks of treatment for major depressive disorder in adults, and to investigate whether antidepressant use is associated with early major cardiovascular adverse events (MACE).

Design

Individual participant data (IPD) network meta-regression and aggregate pairwise meta-analysis.

Data sources

Individual and aggregate level data from randomised controlled trials identified through Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, CINAHL, Embase, LILACS, Medline, Medline In-Process, PsycINFO, the websites of regulatory agencies, and international registers.

Methods

IPD were harmonised to enhance comparability and analysed using network meta-regressions to explore the interplay with baseline QTc, age, sex assigned at birth, body mass index, serum potassium level, and estimated glomerular filtration rate. The primary outcome was changes in QTc Fridericia (QTcF) associated with specific antidepressants and placebo after taking into account modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors. Aggregate data on early MACE were analysed using pairwise meta-analysis comparing antidepressants with placebo.

Eligibility criteria for selecting studies

Double blind randomised trials of adults (≥18 years) with major depressive disorder diagnosed according to standardised, operationalised criteria.

Results

Of 130 unique randomised controlled trials identified, 35 (27%) included individual level data (8679 participants) on QTc with placebo and 10 antidepressants (amitriptyline, bupropion, duloxetine, escitalopram, fluoxetine, mirtazapine, paroxetine, trazodone, venlafaxine, vortioxetine). Compared with placebo, escitalopram and amitriptyline were associated with increased QTc intervals (8.7 milliseconds (ms), 95% credibility interval (CrI) 1.6 to 15.8, and 5.3 ms, 0.8 to 9.8, respectively). When risk factors were considered, amitriptyline and escitalopram were also associated with the highest QTc prolongations (58.8% and 21.3%, respectively), whereas venlafaxine and vortioxetine were often associated with the lowest QTc intervals (24.1% and 9.7%, respectively). Important variability of effects was observed, especially for escitalopram, fluoxetine, and mirtazapine. An aggregate analysis of 139 trials (52 398 participants) did not identify an association between antidepressant use and increased rates of early MACE and non-suicidal death compared with placebo (risk difference 0.01%, 95% CrI -0.01% to 0.02%).

Conclusions

The effect of specific antidepressants on QTc interval differed between adults with depression. No evidence associated antidepressant use with early MACE and non-suicidal sudden death. To support shared decision making and taking into account the trade-off between benefits and harms, individual modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors should be considered when choosing antidepressants.

Systematic review registration

Open Science Framework https://osf.io/c8k65/.
title: QTc changes and early major adverse cardiovascular events associated with antidepressant treatment for major depressive disorder in adults: individual participant data network meta-regression of double blind randomised trials.

authors: Hellemans R, Chesnaye NC, Kramer A, Fu EL, Arnol M, Åsberg A, Bistrup C, Ferraro PM, Heldal K, Helve J, Legeai C, Medcalf J, Nitsch D, Oliveras L, Pérez-Sáez MJ, Ponte B, Savoye E, Segelmark M, Shanmugaranjan S, Sørensen SS, Torra R, Ortiz A, Jager KJ, Stel VS.
summary:
Objective

To quantify the survival benefit of deceased donor kidney transplantation versus continued dialysis according to patients' characteristics (age, diabetes, cardiovascular disease), donor quality (standard criteria donor or expanded criteria donor) and donor retrieval type (donation after brain death or donation after circulatory death).

Design

Target trial emulation.

Setting

European Renal Association Registry data from five countries or regions: Catalonia (Spain), Denmark, France, Norway, and the UK.

Participants

Patients aged ≥20 years receiving dialysis and waitlisted for a first deceased donor kidney-only transplant between 2000 and 2019.

Main outcome measures

Five year patient survival following deceased donor kidney transplantation versus continued dialysis within monthly sequential trials. Flexible parametric spline models estimated adjusted five year patient survival across recipient age.

Results

Of 64 036 waitlisted patients receiving dialysis, 39 244 received a deceased donor kidney transplant: 16 897 (43.1%) from a standard criteria donor/donation after brain death donor, 4324 (11.0%) from a standard criteria donor/donation after circulatory death donor, 14 799 (37.7%) from an expanded criteria donor/donation after brain death donor, and 3224 (8.2%) from an expanded criteria donor/donation after circulatory death donor. Standard criteria donor/donation after brain death and standard criteria donor/donation after circulatory death transplantation showed higher estimated five year survival compared with continued dialysis regardless of recipient age. However, the survival benefit associated with expanded criteria donor/donation after brain death transplantation and, particularly, expanded criteria donor/donation after circulatory death transplantation decreased with increasing recipient age, albeit with greater statistical uncertainty among older patients. For example, among 75 year olds, estimated five year survival following expanded criteria donor/donation after circulatory death transplantation did not differ significantly from that with continued dialysis (59% (95% confidence interval 51% to 66%) versus 55% (54% to 55%); hazard ratio 0.97, 95% confidence interval 0.70 to 1.33), irrespective of diabetes or cardiovascular disease status. This group had a threefold higher early post-transplant mortality than those continuing dialysis.

Conclusions

Standard criteria donor kidney transplantation was consistently associated with a survival benefit compared with continued dialysis. By contrast, the survival benefit associated with expanded criteria donor transplantation declined with increasing recipient age, particularly for expanded criteria donor/donation after circulatory death transplantation, such that the oldest recipients had a smaller and more statistically uncertain estimated survival advantage over continued dialysis.
title: Survival benefit of deceased donor kidney transplantation versus continued dialysis: international target trial emulation.

summary:
Objective

To compare the risk of renal deterioration under treatment with glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists or sodium-glucose contransporter-2 (SGLT-2) inhibitors versus other second line treatments in people with type 2 diabetes with and without albuminuria (albumin to creatinine ratio ≥30 mg/g).

Design

Target trial emulation.

Settings

Linkage of electronic health records and claims data from 10 health systems and two national health insurance plans-data from BESTMED (observational evaluation of second line therapy medications in diabetes) study.

Participants

People with type 2 diabetes and moderate cardiovascular risk and estimated glomerular filtration rate ≥45 mL/min/1.73 m2 on metformin monotherapy who started treatment with a GLP-1 receptor agonist or SGLT-2 inhibitor, a sulfonylurea, or a dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitor after metformin between 2014 and 2022.

Main outcome measure

Deterioration of kidney function defined as doubling of serum creatinine or estimated glomerular filtration rate <15 mL/min/1.73 m2.

Results

Among 75 455 eligible people (61 583 (81.76%) without albuminuria), median age was 60 years (interquartile range 51-68), 36 231 (48%) were women, median haemoglobin A1c was 7.8% (interquartile range 7.3-8.5%), and median estimated glomerular filtration rate was 92 mL/min/1.73 m2 (interquartile range 77-102). People were followed for a median of 32 months (interquartile range 18-57). The estimated five year risk of the renal outcome was 2.4% (95% confidence interval 2.1% to 2.7%) for people taking GLP-1 receptor agonists or SGLT-2 inhibitors versus 2.1% (1.8% to 2.6%) for people taking DPP-4 inhibitors among those without albuminuria; and 3.2% (2.3% to 4.1%) versus 5.4% (4.2% to 6.7%), respectively, among people with albuminuria. The estimated five year risk ratio comparing the GLP-1 receptor agonist or SGLT-2 inhibitor group with the DPP-4 inhibitor group was 1.10 (95% confidence interval 0.90 to 1.38) among people without albuminuria and 0.60 (0.42 to 0.82) among people with albuminuria.

Conclusions

Compared with DPP-4 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists and SGLT-2 inhibitors reduce the risk of deterioration of renal function in people with albuminuria. Little evidence of renal benefit among people without albuminuria was observed over the study follow-up period.
title: Renal outcomes in people with type 2 diabetes with and without albuminuria treated with SGLT-2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists: target trial emulation.

summary:
Objective

To explore how people actively pursuing assisted suicide in Switzerland frame and report the motivations underpinning their decision.

Design

Qualitative exploratory study using semistructured interviews analysed through reflexive thematic analysis within a constructivist framework.

Setting

Participants were recruited across Switzerland between October 2023 and July 2025 through three right-to-die associations and contact with healthcare professionals, including palliative care clinicians and general practitioners. Interviews were conducted in French, German, or Italian and were set in participants' homes or in hospitals.

Participants

30 adults with decision making capacity who were able to communicate verbally and had contacted a right-to-die association to initiate an assisted suicide request were recruited to the study. Participants were interviewed while actively engaged in the assisted suicide request process. Fourteen participants subsequently died by assisted suicide within weeks of the interview.

Results

Participants described the decision to request assisted suicide as the outcome of several motivational processes interacting rather than being caused by a single precipitating factor. Analysis identified six interrelated themes: imagining and shaping one's own death, considering assisted suicide as a trusted commodity, seeking validation and common ground, reclaiming personal power over the medicalisation of dying, crossing the unbearable threshold, and seizing the narrowing window of opportunity. These themes functioned as dynamic, interacting motivations that consolidated, stabilised, and reinforced the choice to pursue assisted suicide over time.

Conclusions

In this study, the pursuit of assisted suicide emerged as prospective, meaning making processes embedded in personal values, relational considerations, and awareness of time, rather than solely as a reactive response to physical suffering. Recognising this complexity may support more ethical clinical dialogue and inform policy discussions in jurisdictions where assisted dying is permitted or under consideration.
title: How patients explain and make sense of their decision for assisted suicide in Switzerland (the Exit Project): qualitative exploratory study.

summary:
Objective

To directly test the generalisability of cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk predictor effects across populations in a high income versus non-high income country, derive comparable risk equations, and identify more effective strategies for prediction across populations.

Design

Population based cohort study.

Setting

Primary prevention cohorts in New Zealand and China.

Participants

Equivalent New Zealand and Chinese cohorts of people aged 30-74 years with diabetes and no CVD based on electronic health records.

Main outcome measures

Country specific five year equations were derived using standardised methods to predict first cardiovascular events; predictor hazard ratios were compared. New Zealand equations were applied to the Chinese cohort, with performance assessed before and after standard recalibration, followed by the updating of predictor hazard ratios that differed statistically significantly.

Results

Between 2004 and 2018, 47 958 New Zealand participants had 5622 (11.7%) first CVD events. Between 2010 and 2018, 46 558 Chinese participants had 3650 (7.8%) first CVD events. Sex specific equations included 16 predictors. Hazard ratios for most predictors were similar between New Zealand and Chinese equations but differed markedly for age (eg, women: 1.61, 95% confidence interval 1.51 to 1.71 per 10 years in New Zealand, 2.51 (2.32 to 2.72) per 10 years in China). Standard recalibration of New Zealand equations did not improve calibration in the Chinese cohort (expected to observed ratio: 0.938 in men, 0.809 in women). Replacing New Zealand age coefficients with Chinese coefficients noticeably improved calibration (expected to observed ratio 1.027 in men, 1.025 in women).

Conclusions

Applying a high income country derived CVD risk prediction equation to a population from a non-high income country with diabetes may introduce systematic errors, primarily driven by differences in the effect of age. Moving beyond simple recalibration to updating key predictor coefficients, particularly age, should be considered for more accurate risk stratification. This study highlights potential limitations of high income country equation updating practices and proposes a feasible approach to improve their accuracy when used in populations from non-high income countries.
title: Simultaneous derivation, validation, and comparison of predictor hazard ratios for cardiovascular risk prediction equations in patients with diabetes from high versus non-high income countries: cohort study.

summary: Skin and soft tissues infections (SSTIs) are common conditions, affecting millions worldwide. SSTIs range from uncomplicated cellulitis to necrotizing fasciitis and can be divided into non-purulent and purulent forms. Non-purulent SSTI is most commonly associated with beta-haemolytic streptococci, while purulent SSTI is typically associated with Staphylococcus aureus Cellulitis most commonly presents with acute warmth, pain, tenderness to palpation, erythema, and oedema. Skin abscess typically presents with a fluctuant tender area with erythema. Laboratory testing is of limited use in most patients. Point-of-care ultrasound is useful for distinguishing cellulitis from abscess if the diagnosis is unclear. Management of SSTI includes antibiotics such as penicillin VK, dicloxacillin, or a cephalosporin, while treatment for skin abscess includes incision and drainage, with antibiotics recommended in select patients. Patients should elevate the affected extremity when possible, and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs may reduce pain and inflammation. The effectiveness of decolonization for patients with recurrent cellulitis or skin abscess is controversial. While most patients with cellulitis or skin abscess are appropriate for discharge with follow-up, patients with sepsis and those with challenges adhering to therapy, immunosuppression, or failed outpatient therapy should be referred to the emergency department. Novel antibiotics such as tedizolid, delafloxacin, omadacycline, and ceftaroline may be considered in select cases.
title: Advances in the diagnosis and management of skin and soft tissue infections.

summary:
Objective

To identify and prioritise potentially inappropriate prescribing cascades based on population prevalence, incidence, and temporal association between the initial and subsequent drug.

Design

Population level retrospective cohort study.

Setting

Health administrative data from a source population of community dwelling older adults in Ontario, Canada.

Participants

2 297 942 community dwelling older adults alive on 1 January 2022.

Main outcome measures

65 potentially inappropriate prescribing cascades were identified through a 2025 international expert Delphi consensus. For each prescribing cascade, the analytic cohort comprised incident users of the initial and subsequent drug combination during the accrual period. The population prevalence of the drug starting the prescribing cascade and the incidence of the initial and subsequent drug combination were measured, and the strength of the temporal association between the initial and subsequent drug was evaluated using adjusted sequence ratios derived from prescription sequence symmetry analyses. Prioritised cascades were those with a population drug prevalence of the initial drug ≥5%, prescribing cascade incidence of ≥1%, and adjusted sequence ratio >1, with the lower limit of the 95% confidence interval (CI) above the corresponding threshold for each measure. Results were stratified by sex.

Results

The cohort comprised 2 297 942 people (54.3% female) aged ≥66 years. Twenty four prescribing cascades (37%) met all three prioritisation criteria. From the prioritised list, cardiovascular drugs were the most prevalent drugs starting the prescribing cascade (drug class range 19.0-65.9%). The highest incidence cascades were iron supplement to laxative (11.9%, 95% CI 11.7% to 12.1%), hydroxymethylglutaryl coenzyme A reductase inhibitor to pain reliever (10.9%, 10.7% to 11%), and cholinesterase inhibitor to sleep agent (10.3%, 9.9% to 10.7%). Temporal association, reported as adjusted sequence ratios, was highest for corticosteroid to antipsychotic (2.55, 95% CI 2.47 to 2.64), laxative to antidiarrheal (2.53, 2.43 to 2.65), and cholinesterase inhibitor to antiemetic drug treatment (2.24, 1.90 to 2.65). The adjusted sequence ratios were consistent when stratified by sex except for the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor or serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor to overactive bladder drug cascade, which was stronger for male older adults (1.21, 1.10 to 1.33) than for female older adults (1.02, 0.96 to 1.09).

Conclusions

This prioritised list of 24 potentially inappropriate prescribing cascades could inform prescribing and deprescribing initiatives and policy development to improve drug safety in older adults at individual patient and population levels.
title: Exploring high priority potentially inappropriate prescribing cascades in older adults: population level retrospective cohort study.
